## Text with numbers and letters

What if we want to pull out just the numbers from those org_codes?

```{r}
library(NHSRdatasets)

data <- NHSRdatasets::ae_attendances

data |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    org_code_number = readr::parse_number(
      as.character(org_code),
      na = c("NA", "Nothing")
    )
  )
```

This does throw up a warning as a number of `org_codes` do not have numbers in
them it also is a little messy, but gives and idea of what can be done

## Filtering data on single letters

Maybe we want to filter our data to any org code that contains a 'R' or a 'P' 
anywhere

```{r}
data |>
  dplyr::filter(
    stringr::str_detect(org_code, 'R') | # note the use of | to denote 'or'
      stringr::str_detect(org_code, 'P')
  )

```

## Over to you

Can you return a dataframe with just the org_codes of those with a number over 50?


```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(
  minutes = 10,
  color_border = "#005EB8",
  color_text = "#005EB8",
  color_running_text = "white",
  color_running_background = "#005EB8",
  color_finished_text = "#005EB8",
  color_finished_background = "white",
  margin = "0.9em",
  font_size = "2em"
)
```

## Answer - 

```{r}
data |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    org_code_number = readr::parse_number(
      as.character(org_code),
      na = c("NA", "Nothing")
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(org_code_number > 50) |>
  dplyr::select(org_code) |>
  dplyr::distinct() # or unique() which is a base R function
```

## Shorten strings

Sometimes we want to shorten strings we can do this by words or characters

```{r}
example <- 'This is an example of a long sentence that I would like to shorten as it is far too long'
```

## Shortening using characters

```{r}
substr(example, start = 1, stop = 15)
```

# Shorten using whole words

```{r}
stringr::word(example, 
              start = 1, 
              end = 4, 
              sep = stringr::fixed(' ')) # note uses end and not stop
```


## Removing words - like for hospital names

Useful for handling really long hospital names and making them readable

```{r}
long_hospital_name <- 'Boggins University HosPital NHS Trust'
```

The capital P is deliberate!

## Change to just 'Boggins HosPital'

```{r}
library(tm)
# tm is a text mining library but has some nice text features

short_hospital_name <- tm::removeWords(
  long_hospital_name,
  c('University', 'NHS', 'Trust')
)

short_hospital_name
```

Close but now we have odd spaces between our words and at the end

## Editing out whitespace

Removes spaces from the start and and of the string as well as the internal spaces

```{r}
squished_short_name <- stringr::str_squish(short_hospital_name)

squished_short_name
```

## Over to you

We still have an annoying rogue capital P in our hospital use your Google 
search skills to find a `str_` function to fix it

We want 'Boggins Hospital'

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(
  minutes = 10,
  color_border = "#005EB8",
  color_text = "#005EB8",
  color_running_text = "white",
  color_running_background = "#005EB8",
  color_finished_text = "#005EB8",
  color_finished_background = "white",
  margin = "0.9em",
  font_size = "2em"
)
```

## Answer - fixing the capital inside a lower case word

```{r}
stringr::str_to_sentence(squished_short_name)

```
